summary: Registers the media types application/gzip and application/zlib for data compressed with the gzip and zlib formats. This lets protocols and software label such content properly. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

eli5.summary: When you send a zipped package, the label on the box should say how it was packed. This memo creates the official labels for two common ways of squishing data.

questions: what is the application/gzip media type
subtitle: Standard labels for data compressed with gzip and zlib.

tldr.problem: Different applications were using non-standard names like application/x-gzip or application/gzip-compressed to label compressed data, creating interoperability confusion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6713 registers two standard media types: application/gzip for gzip compression and application/zlib for zlib compression, both using the DEFLATE algorithm.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use consistent, official media types to label compressed data, improving interoperability.

today: RFC 6713 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The media types application/gzip and application/zlib are now registered with IANA and widely used for labeling compressed content in HTTP, file systems, and protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6713 registers two standard media types for compressed data: application/gzip and application/zlib. Both use the DEFLATE compression scheme, a widely used algorithm for reducing file sizes.

Before this RFC, applications used non-standard names like application/x-gzip, application/gzipped, or application/x-gzip-compressed. This caused confusion because different systems labeled the same type of compressed data differently. By standardizing on two official media types, applications can now communicate unambiguously about compressed content.
sections.eli5: For years, people had made up different names for squeezed files. Now everyone can use the same official names.

sections.title: The Two Media Types
sections.content:
application/zlib labels data compressed with the zlib format, which is designed as a data stream. It includes a header and checksum to detect errors.

application/gzip labels data compressed with the gzip format, which adds more header and trailer fields suitable for files. The first two bytes of gzip data are always 0x1f followed by 0x8b, making it easy for software to recognize.

Both formats implement the same underlying DEFLATE algorithm, so they achieve similar compression ratios. The choice between them is mostly about context: zlib for streaming data between applications, gzip for stored files and web transmission.
sections.eli5: zlib is like vacuum packing—fast, simple, meant for moving things around. gzip is like a properly labeled storage box with extra information written on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compressed data can hide malicious content. Data claiming to be gzip or zlib may not actually be, or its format fields could contain anything including hostile executable code. Applications must treat incoming compressed data with caution and validate it before using it.

The underlying compression formats have their own security considerations documented in RFC 1950, RFC 1951, and RFC 1952.
sections.eli5: A squeezed box could hide something dangerous inside. Always check what comes out before trusting it.
